title: [GitLab] How to prevent leaks from Claude Code's 'Don't ask again' file
summary: This guide details how to find and remove secrets that were inadvertently committed to projects and repositories hosted on GitLab. We’ve confirmed that GitLab’s own infrastructure secrets are protected.In Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent, a developer can approve a shell command by selecting “Yes, and don’t ask again.” Claude then saves that exact command to .claude/settings.local.json in the project folder and runs it without asking in the future. If the command contained a password or a token, so does the file:{ "permissions": { "allow":  } } Claude Code keeps the file out of Git through the developer's personal global excludes, not through the project's .gitignore. That protection lives on one laptop and does not travel with the repository, so the file gets committed and pushed wherever the repository lives. In early November 2026, Apiiro reported that this issue caused 104,185 copies of the file to appear in public repositories, 1,122 of them holding at least one secret. Hundreds more secrets were only in history, in files that had since been deleted.If your developers use Claude Code with repositories hosted on GitLab, this guide shows how to prevent this from happening moving forward, assess exposure now or in the past, and clean every affected project up at once.Prevent: Keep the file out of your repoThere are a few actions you can perform to ensure a developer cannot commit the file by accident, and that if one slips through, you hear about it. There are four layers you can put in place, each a little more work than the last, and the order below is a reasonable one to follow. All of them are settings a group owner changes once; this is the one part of the process GitLab Duo can walk you through but cannot do for you, since its access to GitLab settings is read-only.Start with .gitignoreThe simplest fix is also the one Claude Code should have done for you but does not: a line in each repository's .gitignore that reads .claude/settings.local.json. Claude Code only ever adds the exclusion to the developer's own global git configuration, which stays on that laptop.If you're on Premium or Ultimate, put the same line into the .gitignore in your group's file templates project (in the group, go to Settings > General > Templates), so that every project created from now on inherits it without anyone having to remember.Block the file name with a push rule (Premium and Ultimate)A push rule turns the convention into something GitLab enforces. In the group, go to Settings > Repository > Pre-defined push rules and, under Prohibited filenames, enter:(^|/)\.claude/settings\.local\.json$ From then on, any push that tries to add that file, in the root of the repository or in any subdirectory, on any branch, is rejected before it lands, and the developer sees a message naming the pattern.There are two things to know about how push rules behave, both of which matter here. The rule only checks files being added, not changes to a file that is already tracked, which is why cleaning up the existing copies has to come first. And a rule set on the group is copied into projects created after that moment; it does not reach back to projects that already exist. For those, you set the same rule on each project, either from the project's own Settings > Repository > Push rules or, if you have more than a handful, with a loop over the group's project ids:POST /api/v4/projects/<id>/push_rule {"file_name_regex": "(^|/)\\.claude/settings\\.local\\.json$"} For a project that already has push rules of its own, use PUT on the same path instead; POST will answer 422 Project push rule exists.Add Secret Push Protection for the tokens (Ultimate)The push rule stops the file by name. Secret Push Protection looks at the content of every push, whatever the file is called, and rejects it if it finds a known token format. On GitLab Self-Managed and Dedicated, you first allow the feature for the instance under Admin > Settings > Security and compliance; on GitLab.com, that part is already done. Then you turn it on for each project under Secure > Security configuration > Secret push protection, or for a whole group at once through the group security settings API.Scan everything with one policy (Ultimate)A scan execution policy on the top-level group runs GitLab Secret Detection in every project, including ones that have no .gitlab-ci.yml at all, and individual projects can't switch it off. Create it under Group > Secure > Policies > New policy > Scan execution policy, with one rule that runs on every pipeline and a second that runs on a weekly schedule. The scheduled run looks through history the first time it runs; add the variable SECRET_DETECTION_HISTORIC_SCAN: 'true' to that rule if you want every weekly run to cover full history rather than only new commits. It detects the same token formats as push protection and also covers what is already in the repository, including history when the historic scan is on.Assess: Do you have the file?Once you’ve put the preventative measures in place, you want to know whether .claude/settings.local.json exists anywhere in your repositories, either now or at some point in the past. What the file contains only matters once you have the list of affected repositories, and there are a few ways to get it depending on what your GitLab subscription includes.Ask GitLab DuoIf your group has GitLab Duo (Duo Core on Premium and Ultimate, or GitLab Credits on a Free group on GitLab.com), the quickest route is to open GitLab Duo Agentic Chat, part of the GitLab Duo Agent Platform, in your top-level group and paste this:Has any project in the <GROUP> group ever had a file named .claude/settings.local.json, including projects where the file was later deleted and projects where it only exists on a branch other than the default? For each project, tell me whether it has the file now, and if not, the commit where it was added and the commit where it was removed. Explain how you checked. GitLab Duo works through the group and its subgroups, queries each project's commit history for that exact path, lists the branches of any project with a hit, and fetches the current file to distinguish a copy that is still there from one that was deleted.What comes back is a single table: the project, whether the file is present now, the commits that added and removed it, and a note when a deleted version still held a secret. Forks inside the group are covered along the way, because each fork is a project with its own history, and GitLab Duo finishes by stating what it did not check, such as projects outside the group. Because it reads history rather than a search index, a group of a hundred or so projects takes several minutes, and that same thoroughness is why it finds the deleted copies that a search cannot.If your group has GitLab Orbit, GitLab Duo may use that knowledge graph instead of the search index for the current copies, which brings that part of the answer back in about a minute, with the same results.Search for it yourself (Premium and Ultimate)Without GitLab Duo, the fastest way to find current copies is code search. In each top-level group, open Search, choose the Code scope and tick "Include archived". The query you type depends on which search engine your group runs, and the results page tells you which one that is. Where exact code search is active, which is the case on GitLab.com paid tiers and on Self-Managed instances with Zoekt, turn on regular expressions and search for:file:\.claude/settings\.local\.json$ Where advanced search is active instead, which covers GitLab Dedicated and Self-Managed instances running Elasticsearch, the query is:filename:settings.local.json path:.claude Code search works in one top-level group at a time, including that group's subgroups. If you own several groups, the API makes the loop painless, and the filename: and path: form works there for both engines:GET /api/v4/groups?owned=true&top_level_only=true&per_page=100 GET /api/v4/groups/<id>/search?scope=blobs&search=filename:settings.local.json%20path:.claude&exclude_forks=false&per_page=100 Keep exclude_forks=false because exact code search leaves forks out otherwise. On a GitLab Self-Managed instance with advanced search or exact code search enabled, an administrator can skip the loop and search the whole instance with GET /api/v4/search?scope=blobs&search=filename:settings.local.json%20path:.claude. Use an administrator’s token, because the API only returns projects the caller can see.Whichever engine you use, remember that search shows the default branch as it stands today. A file that was deleted, or that lives on another branch, is invisible to it, which is why the next check exists.Check history (all tiers)A file that was committed and then deleted is still a leak, so for every project you need to know whether the file ever existed on any branch. The commits API answers that, works on every tier and deployment type, and needs nothing to be enabled first:GET /api/v4/groups/<id>/projects?include_subgroups=true&per_page=100 GET /api/v4/projects/<id>/repository/commits?path=.claude/settings.local.json&all=true&follow=false&per_page=100 If the second call returns commits, the content is in that project's history; if it returns an empty list, it never was. This is also the check that finds forks, since they are projects like any other.One detail matters more than it looks: Do not drop follow=false. When all=true is combined with a path, GitLab walks through the newest commits of the whole repository first and only then filters by path, so a repository with more than a page of commits can come back empty even though the file is in its history. With follow=false, the walk is pruned by path from the start and the first page lists every commit that ever touched the file.Check forksEvery fork of an affected project keeps its own copy of the file and its own history, so list the forks with GET /api/v4/projects/<id>/forks and repeat the checks above for each one.Mitigate: Rotate, remove, purgeWhatever secrets you find, the order of operations is rotate, then remove, then purge. Treat every secret the file ever held as public from the date of the first commit that contained it, and rotate it at its provider before you touch the file at all. Deleting the file on its own achieves nothing: The value stays in the repository's history and in every fork until the secret it protects has been changed.Remove the file everywhere at once (with GitLab Duo)Once rotation is underway, open Agentic Chat in the top-level group and paste:In the <GROUP> group, for every project that currently has a committed .claude/settings.local.json on its default branch, open a merge request that removes the file and adds .claude/settings.local.json to the project's .gitignore. Do not merge anything. Skip projects that already have such an open merge request. When done, give me one table: project, merge request link, and the kinds of secrets the file held (no values). Then tell me what remains for me to do across all of them. GitLab Duo finds the affected projects (through Orbit where the group has it, otherwise through search), prepares one commit per project that deletes the file and adds the .gitignore entry. It then pauses twice for your approval: once for all the commits together and once for all the merge requests together, so cleaning up a whole group costs two clicks. When it is done, you get a table of projects, merge request links, and the kinds of secrets each file holds, with no values reproduced, followed by the list of what is still yours to do. All that remains is to review and merge the merge requests.Without GitLab Duo, the same change in each project is three commands:git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json echo '.claude/settings.local.json' >> .gitignore git commit -m "Stop tracking Claude Code local settings" Purge the content from historyRemoving the file only takes it out of the current tree. The old versions stay in the repository until you rewrite history, so do this for every project where the file held a secret, after the secrets are rotated.In the project, go to Settings > Repository > Repository maintenance > Remove blobs, paste the ids of the file's old versions (open the repository tree at an old commit to copy them), and confirm. Then run housekeeping, wait 30 minutes, and prune unreachable objects.Check that it worked: the commit ids after the removed blob change, and the history check from Assess returns nothing for the path. If nothing has changed after a few minutes, check your email, because a failed rewrite is reported only there, to the person who started it.Two cases need care. If the project is a fork, or a public project with forks, the shared object pool keeps the content reachable even after the rewrite; detach the forks first, or clean each repository on its own. And after any rewrite, open merge requests may need a rebase and everyone has to re-clone the repository.SummaryThe TL;DR of this guide is: Ask GitLab Duo whether you have the file, now or in the past. Rotate everything the files held. Ask GitLab Duo to open the clean-up merge requests across the group, review and merge them. Purge history where secrets were. Set the push rule, turn on push protection, add the policy. Two prompts in total, two approval clicks, and a few minutes of settings help ensure that your repositories stay free of this vulnerability.Read moreGitLab Duo Agentic ChatSecret Push Protection and Pipeline Secret DetectionPush rules: prohibited file namesScan execution policiesRemove blobs and repository maintenance

title: [GitLab] How to design a decision-grade pilot for agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI changes the nature of a technology evaluation. When an AI system only generates an answer, a person reviews the output and decides whether to use it. An agent goes further: It gathers context, selects tools, makes decisions, and executes a sequence of actions across the software development lifecycle.The central question for a pilot is therefore not whether the agent can produce an impressive result. It is: What evidence would be sufficient to authorize this agent to perform this workflow for this team?A feature checklist or a collection of successful demos cannot answer that. Leaders need evidence about end-to-end task completion, reliability, control enforcement, level of human effort, operational risk, and economics. This article presents a framework for producing that evidence and turning an agentic AI pilot into a defensible decision.Start with the decision, not the technologyA pilot should begin with the decision it is meant to support. "Evaluate agentic AI" is too broad. A usable decision names the workflow, the users, the proposed level of autonomy, the output the agent must produce, the acceptance criteria and metrics that define success, the quantified outcome the team expects, and the conditions under which it will proceed.For example: Decide whether an AI agent can diagnose selected CI/CD pipeline failures and prepare a merge request with a proposed fix that passes the pipeline’s tests and is accepted by the developer, within defined repository permissions, while reducing total resolution effort by at least 25% against the current baseline.This is more useful than "test an AI pipeline agent" because it fixes the output, the acceptance criteria, the control boundary, and the quantified outcome before anything runs.Define what happens on success, too: a limited rollout with one team, expansion to more teams, and/or a higher level of autonomy. Without an agreed next decision, a pilot drifts into an open-ended experiment.Define the proposed level of autonomyAgentic AI is not simply "autonomous" or "not autonomous." The same agent can operate at different levels of authority. A useful model for a pilot has four levels:Recommend: The agent analyzes the situation and recommends an action.Prepare: The agent creates an artifact, such as a merge request, issue, or remediation plan, but does not apply it.Execute with approval: The agent acts only after an authorized person approves.Execute within boundaries: The agent acts on its own inside a predefined scope and escalates exceptions.Test the level the team could realistically authorize. Evaluating only in recommendation mode says little about whether the agent can safely execute changes. Granting broad autonomy in an early evaluation adds risk without evidence.Autonomy should be earned. A team can start with recommendations, move to prepared changes, and consider bounded execution only after the agent has shown sufficient reliability and control compliance.Evaluate the workflow, not the responseTraditional model evaluation focuses on response quality. Agentic evaluation must focus on completing an end-to-end task.Take an agent that helps resolve a failed pipeline. A plausible explanation is not the outcome. The workflow may require the agent to:Identify the relevant job and logs, and separate the root cause from secondary symptoms.Inspect the right configuration and code, and propose a valid correction without unrelated changes.Create a reviewable artifact and trigger the correct validation steps.Escalate when confidence or authorization is insufficient.Define success at the workflow level: Did the agent reach the intended outcome correctly, within its authority, and with an acceptable amount of human effort? This keeps a convincing explanation from earning a pass when the agent does not reliably complete useful work.Build an evaluation set from representative workA decision-grade pilot needs an evaluation set that reflects the work the agent will actually meet, not scenarios chosen because they show the technology well. For each workflow, include:Realistic tasks: common, well-understood tasks and complex but valid onesDifficult inputs: ambiguous requests with missing or conflicting context, and unsafe or adversarial inputs where appropriateCases the agent must not complete on its own: expected failures, requests outside its authorization boundary, and high-impact actions that require human approvalUse sanitized examples from real workflows whenever possible. Generic exercises remove the dependencies, coding standards, policies, and ownership boundaries that make enterprise work difficult.Add explicit acceptance criteria: a known correct diagnosis, tests that must pass, an expected security policy result, or a rubric completed by a subject matter expert. Without them, reviewers score how persuasive an output looks, which makes results hard to compare and easy to overestimate.Measure a distribution, not the best runAgentic systems behave differently when input, context, or execution state changes, so a single successful run says very little about reliability. AI output is variable and context-dependent, which is why evaluation has to look for patterns across representative scenarios rather than individual results. For agents there is one addition: Variability can affect actions, not only answers.Run important scenarios several times, vary the relevant conditions, and measure:Task outcomes: end-to-end success rate, reviewer acceptance rate, and failure rate by scenario typeHuman involvement: intervention and escalation rate, and rework introduced by the agentControls and resilience: policy or authorization violations, plus latency and recovery from tool, context, or workflow failuresThe goal is not to prove the agent always behaves identically. It is to understand the distribution of outcomes and decide whether it is acceptable for the proposed use. Where predictability is non-negotiable, as in release management, keep the agent out of the execution path. Let it prepare the artifact, such as a deployment script, and let the pipeline run that script, so the execution is deterministic and the agent’s variability is limited to what a reviewer can inspect beforehand. The same pattern works in operations: An agent can assess whether a rollback is needed, while the rollback itself runs as a tested script. In both cases the pilot measures the quality of what the agent prepares or recommends, which are the Prepare and Recommend levels.Two cautions apply. First, aggregates hide risk: A 90% success rate is not strong if the other 10% includes unauthorized changes. Segment results by risk tier and failure type. Second, pilot samples are small, so report counts and uncertainty, not only percentages. Twenty successes in twenty runs does not demonstrate 99% reliability: At 95% confidence, the true failure rate could still be close to 14%. Eighteen out of twenty is consistent with a true success rate anywhere from roughly 70% to 97%. If a threshold matters, size the number of runs to it, or state plainly that the pilot cannot yet support the claim.Set thresholds by risk, and treat controls as hard gatesNot every task needs the same reliability. A wrong explanation that a developer can ignore has a different impact from a wrong production change. Define risk tiers and apply different thresholds to each:Risk tierExample actionEvaluation approachLowExplain a pipeline errorMeasure usefulness and correctness; a human validates the responseMediumPrepare a merge requestRequire passing tests, scoped changes, and reviewer approvalHighMerge or deploy a changeRequire strict authorization, mandatory controls, reversibility, and a substantially higher reliability thresholdSome requirements are not thresholds at all. They are hard gates, and an agent cannot offset a failed gate with time saved elsewhere. Completing the task and respecting the control environment are inseparable: An agent that resolves a vulnerability by bypassing an approval rule has not completed the workflow. Typical must-pass gates include:Identity and authorization: Every action is attributable to the agent and the initiating user, the agent works with least-privilege access, cannot reach tools outside its scope, and retrieves only the permitted context.Policy and approval: Existing security and compliance policies still apply, and required human checkpoints cannot be bypassed.Auditability and control: Reviewers can reconstruct what the agent did and why, high-impact changes can be undone, the team can stop or disable the agent, and failures, policy violations, and abnormal activity are visible.GitLab's guidance on governing agentic AI treats role-based permissions, tool approval guardrails, and human review checkpoints as distinct control points for agent actions. A pilot should verify them with negative tests, not just confirm they exist on paper. Attempt actions outside the permitted scope, remove required context, trigger an approval boundary, and confirm that the agent stops, refuses, or escalates as designed.Measure total effort and cost per successful taskTime saved by the agent is only one side of the equation. An agent can finish a task in minutes and leave a lengthy review. It can cut implementation time while raising the effort needed to understand the change. It can automate routine work and still produce occasional failures that need a senior specialist to diagnose.Measure the whole workflow: preparing requests and context, reviewing output, correcting or reworking changes, handling escalations and failures, and the manual steps avoided. The useful metric is not minutes generated by the agent but total human effort per successfully completed task. Also record where human judgment remains essential. The aim is an effective operating model between people and agents, not necessarily removing people.Apply the same logic to cost. A low-cost execution that frequently fails can cost more than a higher-cost one that completes the workflow correctly. Count model and platform consumption, tool and infrastructure usage, human review, rework and failed attempts, and monitoring and support overhead. Then compare with the current baseline:Cost per successfully completed taskTotal human effort and median time to completion per task, including the share of tasks that need specialist interventionRework or defect rate, and throughput under the same control requirementsThe pilot does not need a perfect financial model. It needs to show whether the value stays credible once the costs a demonstration leaves out are included.Use a decision-grade scorecardA scorecard connects each piece of evidence to the decision the pilot must support. Hard gates are marked "Must pass"; everything else is judged against a target.DimensionDecision questionExample evidenceThreshold typeBusiness outcomeDoes the workflow improve the agreed outcome?Baseline comparison, time and throughput metricsTargetTask successDoes the agent complete the end-to-end task correctly?Acceptance criteria, tests, expert reviewTargetReliabilityAre outcomes consistent across representative scenarios?Repeated runs, success and failure rates segmented by risk, with countsRisk-based targetHuman effortDoes the agent reduce total effort after review and rework?Time study, intervention and escalation rateTargetEconomicsIs the cost per successful task credible at expected scale?Consumption, operations, and support estimatesTargetAuthorizationDoes the agent stay within its assigned permissions?Access and negative test resultsMust passGovernanceAre actions attributable, reviewable, and auditable?Approval records, audit trail, change historyMust passSafety and recoveryCan failures be detected, contained, and reversed?Failure injection, rollback, and disablement testsMust passAdoptionCan the intended users understand and operate the workflow?User observation, feedback, training needsTargetDefine thresholds before running the evaluation. Thresholds set after seeing results let teams adjust the definition of success to match what they observed. Record the evidence behind each result: a score without evidence is hard to defend and gives little guidance for rollout.Worked example: A pipeline failure agentThe numbers below are illustrative, not benchmarks. They show how thresholds, segmentation, and gates combine into a decision.A team wants an agent to diagnose failed pipelines and prepare a merge request with a fix, for developer approval (the Prepare level). They sanitize 30 real failures across three types and run each scenario three times, for 90 runs. Before running anything, they set the following thresholds:Reviewer-accepted merge requests: at least 85% for configuration errors, 70% for flaky tests, and 85% for permission-related failures, where a wrong fix is costlierTotal human effort per resolved failure, including review and rework: at least 25% below the baseline median of 40 minutesHard gates: zero out-of-scope changes, zero bypassed approvals, and every merge request attributable to the agent and the initiating userFailure typeRunsAcceptedRateThresholdResultConfiguration errors302790%85%PassFlaky tests302273%70%PassPermission-related301550%85%FailThe median human effort was 29 minutes against 40, a 28% reduction. The gates held: no violations in 90 runs, and all 10 negative tests ended in a refusal or escalation. Zero violations in 90 runs supports a true violation rate below roughly 3% at 95% confidence, which is evidence but not proof.The resulting decision is narrower than "the agent works." Authorize Prepare-level rollout for configuration errors and flaky tests. Keep permission-related failures at Recommend, fix the context the agent lacks, and repeat that tier. Do not authorize execution.Governed agents across the software lifecycleThe gates above are platform-neutral, but GitLab Duo Agent Platform applies them across the whole software lifecycle instead of to a single tool. For a pilot, that means you can evaluate agents at several stages against one set of controls. Duo Agent Platform offers agents and flows at each stage:Plan: Planner Agent plans, prioritizes, and tracks work, and Data Analyst Agent draws insight from development metrics.Code: Developer Flow turns issues into merge requests, and Software Development Flow builds a multi-step plan before it acts.Review: Code Review Flow automates review tasks and enforces coding standards, and GitLab Duo can also resolve review discussions and merge conflicts.Build and deploy: Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow diagnoses and fixes failing pipelines, and Convert to GitLab CI/CD Flow migrates legacy pipelines.Secure: SAST Vulnerability Resolution Flow generates fixes, the false positive detection flows filter static application security testing and secret detection findings, and Security Analyst Agent triages and analyzes vulnerabilities.These capabilities sit at different points on the autonomy model. Developer Flow prepares a merge request for review, which is the Prepare level. Resolving merge conflicts or review discussions pushes commits, which is closer to execution, so a pilot should hold it to a stricter threshold.The same guardrails apply across all of these stages:Identity: Composite identity is the default for agent sessions. A flow acts through a service account combined with the user who triggered it, and permissions are the more restrictive of the two. Agentic Chat in the UI and IDE is the exception.Approval: Agent tool governance (beta) sets each tool to Always Allow, Always Ask, or Always Deny at group or project level, and project rules can only be equal to or stricter than group rules. By default, write and delete tools ask for approval. Background flows have no user to ask, so their tools can only be allowed or denied, and a tool with no background rule is allowed. Set those rules explicitly, and confirm that enforcement for background flows, which is controlled by a feature flag, is on in your environment.Audit: AI audit events (beta) give a per-session record, with actions attributed to the service account and the human who started the session recorded alongside. Storage is off by default and must be enabled. The AI Governance Dashboard (beta) adds group-level monitoring of agent sessions and developer exposure.Data boundaries: Duo Agent Platform can run with self-hosted models on GitLab Self-Managed, for organizations that must control where model requests are processed.Several of these controls are in beta, so treat them as part of what the pilot evaluates: confirm their status, enable them explicitly, and test them with the negative tests described earlier.Turn the pilot into an authorization decisionA pilot should end with a decision about authority, scope, and operating conditions. Possible outcomes include:Authorize a limited rollout to selected teams, at the evaluated autonomy level or for lower-risk tasks only.Reduce the agent from execution to preparation or recommendation mode, or iterate on controls, context, or workflow design and repeat selected tests.Stop, because value, reliability, risk, or economics are not acceptable.Write the decision down. The record should state:Scope: the workflows and task types covered and excluded, the authorized level of autonomy, and the systems, tools, and data the agent may accessEvidence and controls: the thresholds demonstrated, with run counts, the known limitations, and the controls and approval points that must stay activeOwnership: the workflow owner and escalation path, and the metrics monitored after rollout and the conditions that trigger suspension or reassessmentThis ties pilot evidence to the authority actually delegated. It also stops a successful evaluation of one narrow workflow from being read as approval for broader autonomous use.Start your own decision-grade pilot todayEvaluating agentic AI is an exercise in deciding how much authority a team is prepared to delegate, and under which conditions. The result of a decision-grade pilot should not be "the agent works." It should be a documented decision that states where the agent may act, what evidence supports that authority, which controls must stay in place, and how the team will know when to intervene. That is the standard for moving agentic AI from experimentation into responsible enterprise use.Related resourcesHow to govern agentic AI, MCPs, and AI code assistantsGitLab and Claude Code: Fast, compliant AIGitLab Duo Agent Platform documentation

title: [GitLab] The Pentagon wants to know who checks code when AI writes it
summary: The Department of War now treats AI-generated code as unverified until it’s proven otherwise. DoW Instruction 8430.01, “Accelerated Mission Software,” took effect September 8, 2026, and is the department’s latest guidance on modernizing and managing software. If you build or buy software for the DoW, the instruction changes what’s required of you for every line AI writes. You have to review and test it to the same standard as human-written code, show where AI touched it, and keep it on systems the department has approved. Here’s what the instruction asks of your team, and how GitLab helps you address it.What is DoW Instruction 8430.01?Issued by DoW CIO Kirsten Davies, DoW Instruction 8430.01 applies to every DoW organization and to any acquisition program that includes software, regardless of cost. The instruction sets policy and procedures for modernizing and managing software, with an emphasis on delivering capabilities faster. It directs teams to automate testing and security scanning, reuse what already works, and produce evidence as software is built.The instruction also encourages teams to use AI, calling AI-assisted development a major force multiplier for speed and quality. However, it attaches three conditions: AI’s role is traceable, its code is verified so developers stay accountable, and government data stays within approved boundaries. Each condition changes what a software platform has to do.Three requirements that shape AI in deliveryWhile DoW Instruction 8430.01 covers a wide scope, the three conditions mentioned above show how software platforms must adapt. Here they are in more detail.1. Traceability: Know what AI touchedSoftware on DoW networks needs proof of what’s in it and how it was built. When AI is involved, the proof has to cover AI, too: which models, which versions, and which datasets were used to write or test the code.In GitLab, that record lives beside your code. Dependency Scanning produces your software bill of materials, and audit events and deployment records are generated as part of delivery. Agents in GitLab Duo Agent Platform act through their own service account, tied to the developer who started them, so a commit shows up as the agent acting on behalf of a named person. The commit then lands in the same audit log as everything else, where your SIEM can filter it as AI activity. Because the evidence stays in the platform, you can change models under managed policy without erasing the history.2. Verification: Check what AI writesAccelerated delivery cannot compromise security, safety, or supply chain integrity. AI-generated or AI-modified code is unverified input, and a person must approve changes to security-critical functions (a flaw that lets an attacker in) or safety-critical ones (a flaw that can cost lives or platforms). As the instruction states, “Developers and development teams remain fully accountable for the security, functionality, and integrity of any code generated or modified using AI.”In GitLab, your scans, tests, and approval rules run in the same pipeline for every change, whether a developer or an agent writes the code. Merge request approval policies can require a named reviewer whenever a change touches protected paths or introduces a vulnerability, and protected branches mean an agent can propose but can’t merge past the people you’ve designated.Dependency Scanning Auto-Remediation (currently in beta) is one example of an agent doing the work while your reviewers still sign off. It proposes dependency upgrades and build fixes, and those proposals wait at your existing approval gates like any other merge request. When GitLab orchestrates agents across several steps, a flow can carry a change through review, tests, scans, and approvals on its own, pausing for a human to sign off before a merge or deploy. Every flow runs under the same identity, policy, and evidence chain as the rest of GitLab, so speed doesn’t mean skipped steps. For teams deciding how much autonomy to give agents, the GitLab Security Standard defines five stages (authorize, isolate, verify, release, and respond) that agents must clear before that autonomy is granted. Those stages are mapped to NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) and SP 800-53 controls.3. Data boundaries: Control where AI runsAI systems must respect data boundaries without compromising intellectual property or classified context. Approved AI services must guarantee that government data and prompts aren’t used to train external models, and non-public DoW information stays on approved DoW systems. That means controlling which models are used and where they are hosted.GitLab Duo Agent Platform Self-Hosted runs on infrastructure you control, including air-gapped networks. You choose the supported models, on premises or in a private cloud, and can swap them without rebuilding workflows. Requests route through an AI Gateway you deploy yourself, so prompts and responses stay in your environment. For GitLab Dedicated for Government customers, this is the standard setup: You run the AI Gateway in your own environment, connected to the model provider of your choice.Comply with DoW Instruction 8430.01 todayAI will keep getting faster at writing code. The harder job is showing the code can be trusted, and DoW Instruction 8430.01 asks your team to do exactly that. GitLab keeps that proof with the work: Every AI-assisted change carries its own evidence and audit trail, passes the same gates as human-written code, and runs on models you host and control. Your developers get the same guardrails for AI and non-AI work, without extra tools to learn.See how GitLab Duo Agent Platform helps defense teams keep AI-generated code governed, auditable, and under human control.

title: [Sentry] Monitor your CI performance using Sentry
summary: We use GitHub workflows to make sure our products match our expected quality standards, and by using Sentry Tracing we improved CI run time by 71%. Here's how you can too: Your workflows are slowing you down Writing code and delivering new features is now faster than ever, especially when agents do the work. On the other hand, the build and verification processes become the new bottlenecks of engineering. While the exact setup varies for each developer and project, a standard setup is automated testing in Continuous Integration (CI) pipelines, such as GitHub Actions. With the demand for quality assurance increasing, and feedback cycles taking longer because of slow or failed CI checks, the speed of delivering features slows down. So you start to investigate what exactly is slowing you down. GitHub provides insights into how long your jobs and workflows take in total, but it only surfaces combined run information at any given time, or a sum of all your run minutes. While this is helpful, it does not tell the full story when e.g. the same job takes 9 minutes on one run and 15 minutes on another. Besides that, you also have to actively monitor your run times to make sure they are stable (no flaky tests), and do not increase constantly until all your efforts are wasted. So (if you have the bandwidth) you start to compare multiple runs, structure the data, extract trends manually, and see yourself become a data scientist instead of just delivering the features you initially wanted to. Sentry's distributed tracing can do that work for us: it treats a CI run like any other API request. Investigating CI using Sentry Tracing Each workflow consists of multiple jobs, with each job being a series of sequential steps, each with a different time duration. Using the model behind tracing, these steps can be represented as spans, with full workflows being shown as entire traces, leveraging many features of Sentry such as Explore and custom dashboards. The following screenshot is an example trace of the .NET (macos) job in the build workflow of the Sentry .NET SDK. By opening it up in the trace explorer we can see that the step Build is the longest contributor with ~44 min of the overall ~1 h 23 min. While the actual efforts that can improve workflow duration depend on your type of project and setup, in our case we were able to implement general improvement strategies such as proper caching strategies across runs and parallelizing tests. Bringing it all together we can now open up another trace of the same workflow and see that the Build span is now down to only ~8 minutes, with an overall time of only ~24 min. That makes this job about 3.4x faster, a 71% cut in duration. Gaining visibility using custom dashboards Using a custom dashboard we can now use the collected individual traces and compare the data across multiple jobs, allowing us to easily see p50 and p90 distributions over time, making sure we are not comparing outliers. This shows us that efforts can really pay off as we are now able to say that we reduced the time of workflow runs by about 64%, allowing us to focus time on the right places. Together with the new Sentry CLI we can go another step further and even access the raw data and use it to generate graphs making the gains even more accessible. Bringing it all together we can clearly see the downwards trend as expected: The best part: you can use it too! Collecting traces for GitHub Actions workflows is almost effortless. To get started all you need to do is follow these steps: Create a new project in Sentry, e.g. ci-telemetry or github-actions-ci-data. No worries about picking a platform or alerts for now, as it doesn't matter for this use case. Next, create a private repository named .sentry in the GitHub organization or user account that owns the repositories you want to monitor. Each owner needs its own .sentry repository. In the new repository commit a file called sentry_config.ini and configure the DSN to the project you created earlier:  dsn = https://<key>@<org>.ingest.sentry.io/<project> Finally, install our GitHub App and make sure it can access .sentry and all the workflows you want to monitor in Sentry. Note: our GitHub App can't read your code. It asks for read access to Actions, repository metadata and the single sentry_config.ini file. When a workflow job completes, the app looks up the run's branch, commit and commit author (whose name and email become the event's user), reads your DSN from .sentry, and sends the job to your Sentry project. Feel free to check out the code in the sentry-github-actions-app repository. That's it! One project, one repo, one commit and one app installation and you will start to receive GitHub workflow jobs as Sentry traces*. * Keep in mind that the ingested traces count toward your span quota (or your transaction quota on older plans). Next steps for us at Sentry The GitHub app to collect GitHub Actions workflow telemetry in Sentry should be considered experimental, but now it's your time to shine! Try it out and let us know what works for you, what can be improved, and what you want to see next. The easiest way to make your voice heard is upvoting and commenting on issues in the sentry-github-actions-app repo on GitHub.

title: [Sentry] Finding performance wins in our own traces with a coding agent
summary: For the last few weeks I've used a coding agent to find and fix backend performance issues in Sentry, starting from the traces Sentry sends to itself. Most of the fixes only changed a line or two. But together, they removed hundreds of millions of queries a week, and some expensive lookups became hundreds or thousands of times faster (more details on that below). Pointing the agent at our traces I connected my agent (in this case Claude with Opus 5.5) to the Sentry MCP, pointed it at our own Sentry org and project, and asked it to find hot code path issues similar to a small performance PR I had drafted: use the sentry mcp to look for more similar quick wins around hot path issues things With the latest few model releases, I've found that you don't have to be as specific with how you structure prompts, or make sure that you're controlling context for the agent (for example sharing specific example spans). You can start with something as general as: Find all the critical paths in my application. Use the sentry MCP to find their traces and find ways to optimize them. Based on my initial prompt, the agent sorted spans by how often they ran and how long they took. For each candidate it gave me a file and line, an estimated weekly volume, and a link to an example trace. When the list got thin, I'd point it somewhere new. My prompts were short and mostly questions like: "look for database heavy issues" "is this change risky in any way?" "did you validate the new query using EXPLAIN like we did earlier" "rpc might also be interesting" "i think there's a pr from someone that might already fix this" "lets not touch that area" Then I'd pick an issue and have it investigate further before changing anything. It read the code and the git history and told me what might break. If the fix held up, it opened a draft PR. Sentry is a large codebase, and there are areas I don't know well enough to change confidently. I'd steer the agent away from those, check for work already in progress, and keep looking for something smaller. Making sure the agent has the ability to validate changes in the read-only database rather than guessing leads to much better results. Django SDK instrumentation as a starting point A lot of the Sentry codebase is in Django, and the Sentry Django SDK's automatic instrumentation gave us a good starting point: Django query spans include the SQL as their description. Our traces also include cache calls, cross-silo RPCs, tasks, and API routes. Grouping spans by description gave the agent a way to turn trace data into a ranked list of expensive work. When query-source attributes were available on a database span, they gave the agent the file and line that ran the query. The user_agent attribute showed that one busy endpoint was mostly sentry-cli set-commits --auto paging through an org's repositories on every build. One org had ~16k repositories and was doing this roughly every 40 seconds. That led to a CLI change to avoid the pagination and a server-side index to make the queries cheaper for existing CLI versions. Every PR links an example trace showing the extra query or call, so that it's a bit easier for a reviewer to understand. In one trace, a webhook ran the same 140ms query twice. The result from removing a query was easy to see in a trace. To find out how much it mattered, I also checked request latency and database load in Sentry. Checking query changes For SQL changes, the agent ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after on a read-only database mirror and compared the results. The clearest query cleanup was GroupHistory lookup (GroupHistory records each status change on an issue). The query asked for the newest row across several statuses, meaning Postgres read and sorted every matching row: -- before SELECT * FROM sentry_grouphistory WHERE group_id = %s AND status IN (1, 2, 11, 12, 13) ORDER BY date_added DESC LIMIT 1 -- after: one probe per status, take the max in Python (SELECT date_added FROM sentry_grouphistory WHERE group_id = %s AND status = 1 ORDER BY date_added DESC LIMIT 1) UNION ALL ... For the busiest group on the mirror this went from 935ms to 0.4ms with a warm cache. Results Check that the property exists on the event before running the query during event ingestion. That UPDATE was running ~10k/s on the attachments database in our US region and is now basically gone. Commits on that database fell ~17%, and link_event_to_user_report averaged ~6ms → ~2.5ms. Reuse the already loaded project and skip unnecessary lookups in two hot paths. Reusing the project removed an estimated ~143M extra SELECTs a week. Together, the two occurrence-ingestion fixes brought save_issue_occurrence p50 from ~35ms to ~30ms and p95 from ~95ms to ~61ms versus the same hours the previous day (detector lookup fix). Rearrange the GroupHistory query to use the existing index more efficiently when updating issue status. That query accounted for ~8% of disk reads on the primary database in our EU (Germany) region and ~3% in our US region, and its disk reads fell to nearly zero. Status changes in the occurrence consumer were ~30% faster in the US region and ~13% faster in the EU region versus the same time the previous day. Eager-load the application and token for Sentry app requests to skip round trips later. The two extra selects went from ~1.9% of query volume on the control database to ~0.16%. That works out to roughly 29M fewer queries a day. The fix joins the related objects into two queries we're already making. Add a missing table index for repository pagination. The paginated query alone accounted for ~1.6% of query execution time on the primary database in our US region before rollout. Average database execution fell ~69% (30ms → 9.2ms), with ~52% fewer cached block accesses per query. Requests weren't consistently faster, but they did less database work. Call bulk_set once instead of setting the cache once per issue in results, to reduce round trips. Writing the unhandled flag used to take one cache round trip per issue, about 51ms in the measured example. Batching those writes took one round trip and about 1.2ms. Work around poor Postgres planner performance for a query in detectors. On the database mirror, a query for a small detector fell from 180ms to 0.2ms with a warm cache. Note: Query volumes and daily savings are estimates based on sampled spans and observed traffic. I compared database work per request or query so changes in traffic wouldn't be misrepresented as performance improvements. Trying it on your own app To get started: If you don't already use Sentry, sign up for Sentry Give your coding agent access to the Sentry MCP Prompt your agent to find performance issues in your app. You can start generally and work down to specific areas like: "Find transactions where the same query, with different parameters, runs more than 10 times in a single trace (N+1)." "Find SELECT * or wide queries on hot paths where only a few columns are used." "Find slow queries with ORDER BY ... LIMIT, OFFSET pagination, or LIKE '%...' that likely aren't using an index." Pick an issue and have it investigate further before changing anything. Have it read the code and the git history and assess what might break. Then open a PR. You can also use natural language queries in the Sentry UI's Explore tabs for Logs, Traces, and Metrics to ask things like "Which database queries had the highest P95 duration over the last 7 days?"

title: [Engineering at Meta] Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads
summary: Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017. We’re sharing a few of Intelligent Delivery’s capabilities: how we build ML models to predict the marginal utility of compute, multi-layered mechanisms to move resources across the system, and how we increasingly leverage agentic AI to continuously detect and respond to system shifts. As frontier ads ranking systems advance toward larger models, broader candidate sets, and richer delivery architectures, they also place greater demands on serving efficiency. Compute resources do not scale at the rate that models and system complexity do. The challenge is not just how to build more powerful models, but how to operate them efficiently across a heterogeneous system, with finite serving capacity, and under a tight latency budget. We recently shared how we put idle inference capacity to work. This post covers how we decide where each unit of compute goes to achieve globally optimal system efficiency. Intelligent Delivery is our approach to the problem, and it has contributed an additional ~10% improvement in ads ranking performance on top of model and system advancements across major surfaces, from 2017 through the first half of 2026. It introduces an ML-driven, increasingly AI-operated adaptive optimization layer that continuously directs resources toward the requests, models, hardware fleets, and ranking stages with the highest marginal utility. This helps us run advanced ads ranking models efficiently in production, getting more out of every unit of compute to serve better ads for people who use our apps and services. The Goal and What Makes It Difficult One of our goals is to create a delivery system that continuously converges on its global optimum, regardless of how user behavior changes, models evolve, and the serving stack grows more complex. Three fundamental properties of ads delivery systems make this challenging: The marginal impact of compute is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent: The same additional unit of compute can generate very different returns depending on the product surface, user intent, candidate quality, and system state. Request-aware signals alone are not sufficient; allocating well means estimating, for every request, the return on every available tunable system parameter, where each knob behaves differently at each stage of the funnel. We need to produce a per-request result calculation across a vast decision space within milliseconds. Local optimality does not translate to global optimality: Result estimation is just the start; the serving stack must also be dynamically controllable. Ads delivery spans multi-stage ranking, hundreds of models, generations of hardware, and many data centers. Resources cannot be shifted freely and reliably across these boundaries without adaptive controls that account for complex dependencies throughout the stack. The global optimum is a moving target: The optimization landscape is continuously shifting. Every new model, hardware generation, or new architecture changes the landscape and can invalidate previously optimal allocation decisions. The system needs to adapt quickly enough to retain its optimality. Intelligent Delivery includes three capabilities, each designed to address one of these fundamental system challenges. Capabilities of Intelligent Delivery 1. Request Understanding: A Shared ML Intelligence Layer for Compute Some ad requests benefit more from additional computation than others. Initially, we captured these differences through coarse segments: Requests were grouped by attributes such as surface, context, and ad creative representation, with engineers creating policies to allocate resources for each group. This approach delivered improvements but did not scale. Every new signal multiplied the rules, making the effort unsustainable, and independent segments could not capture the nonlinear interactions among thousands of signals, which limited accuracy. We achieved about a 20% improvement in identifying the highest-impact ad requests in offline benchmarks on major surfaces, relative to our previous production model, after reframing this into two ML problems: Which ad requests are most likely to benefit from additional compute? And how will different resource settings affect their outcomes and serving performance? A side-by-side comparison of static rule-based segmentation, where every request in a bucket gets the same compute, and signal-driven decisions, where an ML-driven predictor sets compute for each request. To answer the first question, we built the Resource Core Model, deep learning models with 6B sparse parameters and 20M dense parameters that run once before candidate retrieval and are shared across the delivery funnel. Learned embeddings and deep feature interactions capture nuanced request patterns that manually defined segments cannot. We then fine-tune the Resource Core Model into a set of specialized models, each generating incremental signals about outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. Together this forms a shared ML intelligence layer for resource allocation: The Resource Core Model understands each request and its serving behavior, while individual mechanisms determine how to translate those predictions into actions. An architecture diagram of the Resource Core Model, showing how dense and sparse request features pass through stacked interaction layers to predict each request’s outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. 2. Allocation Mechanisms: A Hierarchy of Decision Engines Ads serving runs on a globally distributed, heterogeneous fleet with many data center regions, several hardware generations, and millions of hosts, all shared by a multi-tier serving stack. A single allocation mechanism cannot control the complex resource distribution end to end. So we decomposed the problem into a hierarchy of layers and built a dedicated decision engine for each. The easiest way to see the hierarchy is to follow a single request through it. Someone opens their feed. An ad request is created, and over the next few hundred milliseconds it passes through a chain of resource allocation decisions. This leads us to three important questions and answers. Which region serves it? Traffic and capacity are not colocated, and each region carries a different hardware mix and a different amount of headroom — so the same unit of compute is more efficient in some places than in others. We built real-time infrastructure to dynamically shift traffic between regions in a cycle of minutes, driving toward the point where every region achieves the same level of efficiency on its marginal unit of capacity. What hardware does it land on? Our fleet spans CPUs from Intel, AMD, and Arm and accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and our own Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA), across several generations of each. The hard part isn’t the variety; it’s that capacity isn’t interchangeable. Our stages are bound by different resources — retrieval by memory capacity, ranking by compute, and model inference by accelerator throughput — so there is no single fastest SKU, only a best match per workload. We benchmark measured efficiency for every workload-SKU pair, then solve the assignment so that scarce hardware goes to the workloads that convert it into the most useful work. Inside the host, how much of this machine does the request get? Concurrent requests differ in latency budget and impact, under a hard tail-latency SLO. We predict each request’s expected outcome and its compute and latency cost in real time using our advanced deep learning models, and solve a constrained optimization that maximizes impact delivered within the host’s latency budget — as the host load increases, the performance trade-off rises and resource-intensive low-impact work is trimmed first. Enforcing those decisions takes control across the whole stack, so the framework spans from kernel-level scheduler up to application-level thread pools. A three-step flowchart following one ad request through the decision hierarchy: which region serves it, which hardware it runs on, and how much of the host it gets. These three steps are just a subset of the allocation decisions we make during a request’s lifecycle. Following this, we optimize the number of ads to rank for each request in each ranking stage, what ad candidates enter the pool, and much more. These allocation decisions are tightly coupled, so a resource change in any one of them ripples across the whole system. Shifting traffic between regions changes per-host load, which drives the feedback controller that sets how much work each request gets. We validate these changes in an end-to-end, closed-loop hardware testing environment to make sure we are optimizing for the global optimum instead of a local optimum. 3. Optimization Loop: Self-Optimizing Serving with Agentic AI As our ad system advances, productionizing a new model, a new mechanism, or new hardware into the system requires a lot of effort to achieve seamless integration. We can’t brute-force every single configuration across millions of tunable dimensions built in our system for a new change. That would require too much time and far more hardware resources than we have. We relied heavily on human expertise and engineers’ prior knowledge to identify promising configurations. But this approach didn’t scale, because every new model, mechanism, and hardware generation expanded the search space faster than engineers could explore it. We tried automating this with a constrained optimization approach, which delivered improvements but remained inflexible and slow. We found that it lacked the ability to generalize (it could only cover a few key knobs) and couldn’t effectively incorporate human intuition from prior experience. Instead of doing a blind search, AI agents continuously monitor the entire system landscape, identifying changes and inefficiencies to address. In a long context window, an agent reads mechanism source code, design documents, and a decade of experiment logs and narrows that to a handful of changes worth testing. Engineers review and approve the final change before it ships. Today, agents can already propose well-reasoned changes and design and run rigorous experiments. In the first half of 2026, agents contributed to about 20% of Intelligent Delivery optimizations. On our most automated mechanism, they now contribute to about 80% of the engineering effort, from understanding the system landscape and forming hypotheses to running experiments and converging on the final change. This shortens the optimization loop from months to weeks while keeping people firmly in control. And it steadily captures the expertise engineers have built over the years. A loop diagram of the AI-driven optimization cycle, where agents collect data, propose changes, and run experiments, with an engineer approving every change and a shared knowledge base feeding each step. The Next Frontiers for Intelligent Delivery End-to-end real-time optimization: Today, understanding a request and deciding how to serve it are still two separate steps. We’re building toward fusing them into a single model that reads a request and serves it in real time, without months of experiments. There’s established work in varying compute per request with learning-based methods. However, doing it jointly across every serving stage at once — under shifting traffic, hard capacity limits, and tight inter-stage dependencies — is the part that’s still open, and it’s what we’re pushing on. Serving state-of-the-art models on GPUs: Large ranking models, like Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM), are growing toward LLM scale and increasingly run on GPUs, which opens a different optimization space. GPU capacity doesn’t divide the way CPU time does — it comes in whole, fixed blocks, and throughput, batching, and memory all behave differently. The levers we built for a CPU world have to be reimagined, and much of our work now goes into understanding those mechanisms and turning them into new levers. The more useful work we get out of each accelerator, the more people we can serve with strong models under the same capacity. title: [Engineering at Meta] Your Algorithm: Giving People More Ways to Personalize Facebook Recommendations
summary: Your algorithm is a suite of AI-powered tools that makes Facebook recommendations more transparent and steerable, with a single editable view of the interests that shape Feed and Reels. We’re sharing how Your algorithm turns people’s natural language preferences into responsive recommendations, and how LLMs are tailored to specific tasks within the system. Traditionally, the recommendation systems behind what people see on Facebook have learned from implicit engagement signals. While this allows them to scale well, it also means they adapt slowly and capture little nuance. But what if people could interact directly with the algorithms that rank and recommend what they see to instantly make their recommendations more personal and customized? Your algorithm is an end-to-end system that addresses the limitations of adaptability and nuance in recommendations. This new suite of AI-powered tools lets people on Facebook state, in their own words, what they want to see in their Feed and Reels. By tasking a collection of large language models (LLMs) with understanding, storing, and tracking people’s stated preferences along with their user behavior, we’ve created a recommendation system that responds to people’s preferences and adjusts the content they see. An Overview of the Your Algorithm System Architecture The Your algorithm page has three parts (Figure 1): At the top, a one-sentence Lately Summary that describes recent viewing activity. Below it are two lists: “Interested In,” prefilled with interests inferred from past activity. “Not Interested In,” capturing topics the user has explicitly marked as not interested, or has X-ed out or hidden on Facebook. People can use the interface to add interests (using natural language), move them between lists, or remove them. Every change applies responsively to both Feed and Reels, and will further update as the person gives feedback on individual posts. Figure 1: The Your algorithm page. Your algorithm system has several components that cover the full lifecycle of a preference, from inferring and validating it to applying it in ranking and delivery (Figure 2). Profile generation builds the initial interest profile. Preference management validates each change, enriches it with the signals ranking needs, and saves it to a single store that both Feed and Reels read, ensuring that the preferences shown on the page are the same ones used in ranking. Ranking applies the “Interested In” and “Not Interested In” lists throughout the funnel. Delivery optimization helps each change take effect more responsively. Figure 2: An overview of the Your algorithm system. From Preferences Into Recommendations Turning a stated preference into recommendations poses three distinct problems. An interest added to Interested In needs to deliver relevant content quickly, without crowding out everything else. An interest added to Not Interested In needs to hold reliably, even though topics are fuzzy and any single filter misses some matches. And both need to take effect responsively, even when the next recommendations were cached before the change. Your algorithm addresses each problem with dedicated logic across the recommendation funnel, from retrieval through reranking to the device (Figure 3). Interested In: Surfacing New Interests Without Flooding Each interest in Interested In drives four dedicated retrieval sources. Two find matching content directly (through search and through clusters of closely related topics), and two extend reach through the content graph and item-to-item similarity. Retrieving explicitly for each interest ensures enough relevant candidates for downstream ranking. This is important because, without it, content about a brand-new interest might never enter the ranking pipeline at all. Candidates that pass a relevance check, which compares the meaning of the interest with each candidate, receive a promotion in late-stage ranking so they can compete alongside other content. A control layer in reranking then determines where they appear. Responsiveness alone is not the goal. Our approach emphasizes balance over volume: A new interest should show up, not take over. The control layer spaces out recommendations for the same interest and caps each interest’s daily contribution. Retrieval also fetches candidates for only one interest per request, so every interest gets a turn. New interests receive extra weight for a limited period. After that, the recommendation system learns from how people engage with that content. Not Interested In: Layered Filtering at Every Stage Interests in Not Interested In are enforced at several stages based on different signals to achieve high precision and recall. During ranking, the same embedding-based comparison used in the relevance check removes candidates too close to an interest in Not Interested In, and demotion rules push down near matches. After ranking, the LLM reranker reviews the final list. On the device, cache invalidation, described below, removes matching candidates that are already queued for display. Not every entry in Not Interested In is about a topic. Quality-related requests, such as reducing AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, map to dedicated demotion signals rather than topic matching. When a request names a creator, that creator’s content is filtered out directly. Responsiveness Optimization Even with ranking tuned to respond to preferences, there is still room to improve how responsively a change reaches what people see. Content for a new preference is not picked up until the next fetch request, and content already cached on the device was ranked before the preference was set. We added two delivery mechanisms to close these gaps. When a new interest is added to Interested In, the system sends an extra fetch request outside the normal fetch cycle, called a supplementary tail load, to retrieve fresh recommendations so matching content appears quickly. When an interest is added to Not Interested In, cache invalidation handles candidates ranked before the change. The client obtains the new interest’s clusters and drops any cached content that matches them before it is displayed. Figure 3: Where Your algorithm preferences act in the content ranking funnel. LLMs Across the Preference Lifecycle: From Profile to Final Check LLMs play a role at several key points in a preference’s life in Your algorithm. They generate the initial profile that people see on a first visit, validate each change as it is made, and give the final recommendations a last check against interests in Not Interested In (Figure 2). Each use comes with its own constraints, including latency, serving capacity, and safety, and evaluating them requires a new approach as well. Profile generation provides the starting content for a first visit: the inferred interests and the Lately Summary. An LLM turns interest signals, which are refreshed regularly, into a set of inferred interests with clear, readable topic names. These are prefilled in the Interested In list and reflect past viewing across Facebook Feed and Reels. The LLM also writes the Lately Summary, a sentence that highlights ongoing interests. Together, they provide a recognizable starting point that is easy to review and correct. Every edit on the Your algorithm page passes through preference management. When an interest is added or moved, an LLM checks that the phrase is a coherent topic, detects duplicates, and maps it to a clean topic name. This step runs on a smaller model that is efficient to serve at scale. The validated interest is then enriched with the signals ranking needs, such as an embedding and search keywords, and saved to the shared preference store. The LLM is only one layer of validation. The system also has a dedicated component that performs integrity and safety checks. Once recommendations are ranked, LLM reranking provides a last check against interests in Not Interested In. The ranking funnel matches interests to candidates using embeddings, which are fast but coarse. To catch what they miss, a fine-tuned LLM reviews the ranked list and removes content it judges to be related to an interest recently added to Not Interested In. A key insight was that a small model fine-tuned to return only the items to remove was faster and more reliable than a general-purpose model judging each item individually. Evaluating these LLM calls required its own approach. Standard offline metrics cannot tell whether a Lately Summary is accurate or whether the reranker removed the right candidates, so a separate LLM acts as a judge, grading each call’s output against expected behavior. This provides an objective, repeatable way to compare prompts and models before launch. The Future of Your Algorithm Your algorithm creates a more transparent and personalized recommendation experience, informed by both behavior and stated intent. But there are important opportunities remaining, such as better interpreting ambiguous input and making recommendations respond even more precisely to each request. We are also exploring additional entry points so that preferences can be shaped from more places.
